claims.text: In CoCrFeMnNi, toughness retention under demanding conditions is governed by an optimum nanoscale precipitate state.
A critical range of precipitate size, spacing, and coherency modulates dislocation motion.
Insufficient or excessive precipitate coarsening disrupts dislocation mobility and causes toughness loss.
The as-processed CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a metastable distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Conventionally processed CoCrFeMnNi has a dual-phase or predominantly single-phase matrix.
Varying aging temperature and time can tune precipitate size, spacing, and coherency in CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed alloy should be tested at high strain rate or elevated temperature to represent demanding service conditions.
Nanoscale precipitate characteristics control local dislocation pinning and mobility.
Optimal precipitates prevent excessive dislocation pile-up and associated stress concentrations.
Preventing excessive dislocation pile-up promotes uniform plastic deformation and retention of toughness.
Over-aging produces coarser or more widely spaced precipitates.
Coarse or widely spaced precipitates either fail to pin dislocations effectively or act as crack-initiation sites.
Specimens within the proposed optimum precipitate range will have greater fracture toughness and ductility than the as-processed baseline.
Under-aged and over-aged specimens will have lower toughness than specimens in the optimum precipitate state.
The as-processed baseline has a less optimized precipitate distribution than the proposed optimally aged state.
The proposed relationship applies only while precipitate evolution is the predominant microstructural change and substantial secondary phase transformation or grain growth is absent.
The proposed relationship may cease to apply at very low temperatures or ultrahigh strain rates where deformation mechanisms other than dislocation-based plasticity dominate.
Grain-boundary characteristics and residual stresses may alter the optimum precipitate size and spacing.
TEM or SEM can quantify precipitate characteristics and dislocation configurations, while mechanical tests can measure fracture toughness and elongation.
The hypothesis is falsified if substantially different precipitate states have similar toughness and ductility or if the proposed optimum state does not outperform the baseline.
